speaker: Mario Zechner
main_topic: Building a custom, self-modifying AI coding agent called 'pi' to counteract the bloated, unreliable, and spammy nature of current commercial coding agents.

key_claims.claim: Commercial coding agents like Claude Code have become bloated and unpredictable.
key_claims.details: They added unnecessary features like complex rendering (acting like a 'game engine'), which introduced bugs, flicker, and broke existing developer workflows.

key_claims.claim: We are currently in the 'fuck around and find out' phase of coding agents.
key_claims.details: The current forms of coding agents are not the final forms; the industry is still experimenting to find what actually works.

key_claims.claim: Agents need to be self-modifying and adaptable to individual workflows.
key_claims.details: Instead of developers adapting to rigid tools, agents should have a minimal core that can be extended, modified, and hot-reloaded by the agent itself based on user instructions.

key_claims.claim: Unsupervised agents ('clankers') are destroying the open-source ecosystem.
key_claims.details: Automated agents are spamming repositories like OpenClaw with thousands of low-quality, AI-generated issues and pull requests, overwhelming maintainers.

key_claims.claim: Agents compound errors ('booboos') because generation speed outpaces human review.
key_claims.details: Because agents can generate vast amounts of code quickly, humans cannot review it all. This leads to compounding mistakes, unmaintainable codebases, and a loss of understanding of how the system works.

key_claims.claim: Agents are 'merchants of learned complexity' and make poor architectural choices.
key_claims.details: They learn from the internet, where 90% of code is 'old garbage.' Because their context is local, they patch things locally but break systems globally, introducing massive technical debt.

key_claims.claim: Humans must remain in the loop to feel the 'pain' of bad code.
key_claims.details: Friction and pain drive humans to refactor, simplify, and truly understand systems. Agents do not feel pain and will happily continue adding garbage to a codebase.

frameworks.name: The 'pi' Architecture
components: pi-ai: Unified LLM API with 15+ providers, streaming, tool calling, and cross-provider context handoff.
pi-agent-core: Agent loop, tool execution, validation, event streaming, and message queuing.
pi-tui: Terminal UI framework featuring differential rendering and synchronized, mostly flicker-free output.
pi-coding-agent: The CLI, handling session management, themes, extensions, skills, and project context.

frameworks.name: Properties of Good Agent Tasks
components: Scoped: The agent doesn't need to gobble up tons of code to succeed.
Closed loop: The agent can evaluate its own work.
Not mission critical: Best for dashboards, debugging tools, etc.
Boring stuff: Tasks you would never have time to try.
Reproduction cases: Sifting through user issues to recreate bugs.
Rubber ducking: Bouncing ideas off the agent when a human isn't available.

examples.lesson: Adding complex UI rendering features to a terminal tool introduced bugs and broke workflows, showing that unnecessary complexity undermines core utility.

examples.example: OpenCode's context pruning and LSP integration.
examples.lesson: Silently removing tool outputs to save tokens, or forcing the agent to check for errors before finishing its thought, confuses the model and breaks its context.
A highly minimal benchmark that only sends keystrokes to tmux outperformed complex, native agent harnesses, proving that simpler tools often yield better agent performance.
The repo received over 5,000 issues and 5,000 PRs, largely generated by 'clankers', illustrating that unsupervised agents require human-in-the-loop bottlenecks to prevent OSS degradation.
By providing a highly extensible core with hot-reloading, users can build wild, custom extensions (like playing games in the terminal) proving the flexibility of a self-modifying agent.

terminology.definition: Low-quality, unrefined, or poorly generated AI content and code.
A derogatory term for unsupervised, poorly functioning AI agents that spam issue trackers and submit garbage pull requests.
The speaker's colloquial term for errors, bugs, or mistakes introduced into a codebase by AI agents.
The wrapper, environment, or system used to run and interact with the underlying AI model.

takeaways: Retake control of your tools and workflows; build your own agents if necessary.
Do not trust agents with mission-critical architecture or APIs; write them by hand.
Implement human bottlenecks, such as forcing contributors to write issues in a human voice, to filter out agent spam.
Cap generated code to an amount you can realistically read and review.
Embrace the friction of coding, as it is necessary for building understanding and taste.
Slow down, think about what you are building and why, and learn to say 'no' to unnecessary features.

notable_quotes.quote: I build pi in a world of slop.
We are in the fuck around and find out phase of coding agents.
Clankers are destroying OSS as we know it.
Agents are actually compounding booboos, which is my word for errors, with zero learning and no bottlenecks.
Know what we call a sufficiently detailed spec? A program.
Slow the fuck down. Think about what you're building and why.

statistics: The 'pi' agent uses only 4 tools: read, write, edit, bash.
The token budget for pi's system prompt and tools is < 1,000 tokens, compared to ~3,000 for OpenCode and ~7,000-10,000 for Claude Code.
The OpenClaw repository accumulated 5,000+ issues and 5,000+ pull requests due to agent spam.
Enterprise-grade codebase complexity can be reached in just 2 weeks using 2 humans and 10 agents.
The speaker estimates that 90% of code on the internet, which models learn from, is 'old garbage.'
